title: Reading practice: Garden Beds and Bus Plans
description: A data table about garden beds and a word problem about two bus plans: read data, explain math steps, and judge claims and evidence.

stimuli.title: Class Garden Bed Records
stimuli.caption: Records for four garden beds after three weeks. All four beds used the same soil and the same amount of water.

stimuli.title: Two Bus Plans
paragraphs: Room 8 is planning a trip to the science museum. There are 45 students and 5 adults, so 50 people will go. The class can choose between two bus plans.
Plan A uses small buses. Each small bus holds 10 people and costs $40. Plan B uses large buses. Each large bus holds 25 people and costs $90.
Nadia reads the plans first. “We should choose Plan A,” she says. “One small bus costs only $40, and one large bus costs $90.”
Ben shakes his head. “I see it differently, Nadia. A bus that costs less does not mean the plan costs less. We have to count how many buses we need first.”
Nadia thinks about it. “That is a good idea, Ben. You are right that I should count the buses. Then I will check the total cost.”
Ms. Reyes smiles. “Please use numbers to support your choice.”

items.stem: Which sentence correctly describes Bed C?

options.text: Eight carrot seeds were planted, and ten became healthy seedlings.
Ten bean seeds were planted, and eight became healthy seedlings.
Ten carrot seeds were planted, and eight became healthy seedlings.
Ten carrot seeds were planted, and they got two hours of sun.

distractors.a: The numbers are swapped. Bed C had 10 seeds planted and 8 healthy seedlings.
distractors.b: Bed C grew carrots, not beans.
distractors.d: Bed C got 6 hours of sun each day. Two hours is Bed D.

items.explanation: In the Bed C row, the plant is carrots, 10 seeds were planted, and 8 became healthy seedlings.

support.clue: Find the row that begins with Bed C. Then read across, one column at a time, and match each number to its column heading.
support.frame: In Bed C, ______ seeds were planted and ______ became healthy seedlings.
support.model:
Mentor example (a different table). A table about a class bake sale says: Tray 1, Cookies, 24 made, 20 sold. A correct sentence is “Tray 1 had 24 cookies made, and 20 were sold.” Start at the row name, then read each column heading and its number.

Now read the Bed C row the same way.

misconceptions.a: swaps two numbers in the table

items.stem: Complete the explanation. Choose the best word or number for each blank.

dropdown.template: In Bed A, {1} of the 20 bean seeds became healthy seedlings. In Bed C, {2} of the 10 carrot seeds became healthy seedlings. Because 16 out of 20 and 8 out of 10 are {3} fractions, the two beds did equally well.

items.explanation: Bed A had 16 healthy seedlings and Bed C had 8. Doubling 8 out of 10 gives 16 out of 20, so the fractions are equivalent.

support.clue: Use the column “Healthy seedlings” for the first two blanks. For the last blank, compare 8 out of 10 with 16 out of 20 and ask how the numbers are related.
support.frame: ______ out of ______ and ______ out of ______ are ______ fractions.
support.model:
Mentor example (a different data set). In a game, Team Red won 6 out of 12 rounds and Team Blue won 3 out of 6 rounds. Doubling 3 out of 6 gives 6 out of 12, so the two amounts are the same size and the teams did equally well.

Now explain Bed A and Bed C with the same kind of sentence.

facts: 16 out of 20 and 8 out of 10 are equivalent fractions (both equal 4/5).

items.stem: Match each pair of beds with the sentence that explains what the table shows about them.

right.text: Both grew carrots, and the bed with more sun had more healthy seedlings than the other.
Both grew beans, and the bed with more sun had more healthy seedlings than the other.
The plants were different, but both beds had the same sun and the same fraction of healthy seedlings.
Bed D had the most healthy seedlings, so two hours of sun is the best amount for plants.

items.explanation: Beds A and B both grew beans (16 and 10 healthy seedlings). Beds C and D both grew carrots (8 and 5). Beds A and C had 6 hours of sun, and 16 of 20 equals 8 of 10.

support.clue: For each pair, check three columns: Plant, Hours of sun, and Healthy seedlings. Say what is the same and what is different.
support.model:
Mentor example (a different comparison). Two bike riders both rode for one hour. Rider 1 rode a hill path and went 8 miles. Rider 2 rode a flat path and went 12 miles. A good sentence is “Both riders rode for one hour, but the rider on the flat path went farther.”

Now state what is the same and what is different for each pair of beds.

facts: 16 out of 20 and 8 out of 10 are equivalent fractions (both equal 4/5).

items.stem: A student claims: “The hours of sun changed how many seedlings stayed healthy.” Which two pieces of evidence best support this claim?

options.text: Bed A got 6 hours of sun and had 16 healthy bean seedlings, but Bed B got 2 hours and had only 10.
Bed A and Bed C both got 6 hours of sun each day, and many healthy seedlings grew in both beds.
Bed C got 6 hours of sun and had 8 healthy carrot seedlings, but Bed D got 2 hours and had only 5.
Bed A had 20 seeds planted in it, while Bed C had only 10 seeds planted in it.

distractors.b: Two beds with the same sun cannot show that sun made a difference. The claim needs beds with different sun.
distractors.d: The number of seeds planted is not about sun, so it does not support the claim.

items.explanation: A claim about sun needs beds with the same plant and different sun. Beds A and B (beans) and Beds C and D (carrots) show more sun with more healthy seedlings.

support.clue: A claim about sun needs a comparison. Look for pairs of beds with the same plant but different numbers in the sun column.
support.frame: The evidence that ______ shows that ______ because ______.
support.model:
Mentor example (a different claim). A student claims, “Warm water melts ice faster.” Good evidence compares two cups of ice: ice in warm water melted in 5 minutes, but ice in cold water melted in 12 minutes. A comparison where only one thing changes is strong evidence.

Now choose the evidence that compares beds in the same way.

misconceptions.d: uses a fact that is not about the claim

facts: 16 out of 20 and 8 out of 10 are equivalent fractions (both equal 4/5).
Plants need sunlight to grow into healthy seedlings.

items.stem: Ben says to count the buses first. Put these steps in an order that makes sense for finding Plan A’s cost and comparing it with Plan B.

items.text: Compare the total cost of Plan A with the cost of Plan B.
Divide 50 people by 10 seats on each small bus to find 5 buses.
Add 45 students and 5 adults to find 50 people.
Multiply 5 buses by $40 to find the total cost of $200.

items.explanation: You must know how many people are going before you can find the number of buses. You need the number of buses before you can find the cost, and the cost before you can compare.

support.clue: Ask which number you need before you can do the next step. You cannot find the cost until you know how many buses there are.
support.model:
Mentor example (a different problem). To find how many boxes of crayons a class needs: First, count the students. Next, decide how many crayons each student gets. Then divide the total number of crayons by the number in one box. Each step uses the answer from the step before it.

Now put the steps for Plan A in an order that makes sense in the same way.

items.stem: Which sentence is the best reason that Ben disagrees with Nadia?

options.text: Large buses always cost less than small buses, so Plan B wins no matter how many buses we need.
Plan A needs only two buses, so it must cost the least, and the number of people does not matter.
Nadia forgot that the adults have to pay for their own seats on the bus, so the total is wrong.
One cheaper bus does not make a cheaper plan, because the plans need different numbers of buses.

distractors.a: A large bus costs $90 and a small bus costs $40, so a large bus does not cost less.
distractors.b: Plan A needs 5 small buses because 5 buses hold 50 people.
distractors.c: The passage never says anyone pays for a seat. The cost is for each bus.

items.explanation: Ben says that a cheaper bus does not make a cheaper plan. You first have to count how many buses each plan needs.

support.clue: Find Ben’s two sentences. Ask what Ben says Nadia must do before she chooses a plan, then check each choice against the numbers in the plans.
support.frame: Ben disagrees because Nadia looked at ______, but she did not think about ______.
support.model:
Mentor example (a different argument). A student says, “Brand X pencils are cheaper, so buy them.” A classmate answers, “One pencil costs less, but Brand X comes in packs of 4 and Brand Y in packs of 12, so we must compare the cost of each pencil, not each pack.” The reason points to a missing piece of information.

Now find the choice that points to the missing information in Nadia’s idea.

misconceptions.b: uses a number that does not fit the problem
misconceptions.c: adds a detail that is not in the text

items.stem: A student writes a short argument for the class. Sort each sentence: is it a claim or evidence?

tokens.text: Plan B needs 2 large buses, and 2 × $90 = $180.
Plan A needs 5 small buses, and 5 × $40 = $200.
Plan B is the less expensive plan for our class.

items.explanation: A claim tells what someone thinks. Evidence gives numbers that can be checked: 2 × $90 = $180 and 5 × $40 = $200.

support.clue: Evidence has numbers you can check. A claim is a sentence that says what is best, with no calculation inside it.
support.frame: The claim is that ______. The evidence is that ______.
support.model:
Mentor example (a different argument). Claim: “The library is the quietest room.” Evidence: “At noon, the library had 2 people talking, but the cafeteria had 40.” The claim says what is true. The evidence gives a number to check.

Now sort the sentences into claims and evidence in the same way.

items.stem: Sort each sentence from the conversation: does the speaker agree or disagree?

tokens.text: A bus that costs less does not mean the plan costs less.
That is a good idea, Ben.
You are right that I should count the buses.

items.explanation: Ben says “I see it differently” and explains why Nadia’s idea is not complete. Nadia then says “That is a good idea” and “You are right,” which show agreement.

support.clue: Look for signal phrases. Some words and phrases open a different opinion, and others accept a classmate’s idea.
support.frame: When I say “______,” I ______ with my classmate.
support.model:
Mentor example (a different talk). Two students plan a poster. One says, “I see it differently; the title should be bigger.” The other says, “That is a good point.” The first sentence disagrees politely. The second sentence agrees.

Now sort the sentences from Ben and Nadia in the same way.
